title: Title: I'm trying out development with ChatGPT (with Codex) and Claude Code. Am I approaching this the right way, or just overcomplicating things?
author: Thrustherx
selftext:
I'm currently learning game development using Godot, Blender, ChatGPT, and Claude Code. I'm not here to promote a game. I'm genuinely trying to understand whether my workflow makes sense.

I started by discussing game concepts and mechanics with ChatGPT, then using Claude Code to implement and test them. We've gone through several prototypes, changed direction more than once, and gradually built a tower defense project.

Over time, the workflow became more structured:

* **ChatGPT:** My planning partner. We discuss ideas, question design decisions, review Claude's results, and prepare implementation tasks.
* **Claude Code (Sonnet):** Most of the coding, implementation, debugging, and testing.
* **Claude Opus:** More difficult architecture, research, and technical decisions.
* **Me:** I make the final decisions, test the game, evaluate visuals, and decide what needs changing. Sometimes use Haiku or Fable if needed.

Instead of asking AI to build everything at once, we've divided the work into smaller areas: gameplay systems, balancing, map editing, asset generation, animations, and visual effects.

We also started using documentation, milestone reports, automated tests, Git checkpoints, and explicit approval before major changes.

**One interesting problem has been context management.**

I've already had to close two extremely long ChatGPT conversations because they became unwieldy. We now rely more on project documentation, handoff summaries, and separate Claude Code sessions rather than expecting an AI to remember everything.

We've built quite a few experimental tools and systems, but I've also noticed some problems.

Sometimes we spend too much time planning or building tools instead of actually making the game. Recently, we spent multiple iterations trying different procedural character-modeling techniques. The code worked and the tests passed, but the characters still didn't look good. Eventually, we documented what we'd learned and stopped.

That's made me question whether I'm learning good development practices or just getting better at managing AI agents. Also, I've been trying to apply the posts I've been seeing only about how to reduce token usage, keep the project organized etc.

**I'd really appreciate some honest advice:**

* Is splitting AI work into separate responsibilities and small tasks actually a good approach?
* How do you prevent AI-assisted projects from becoming overengineered?
* How much documentation and testing is reasonable for a solo learning project?
* How do you manage context across long conversations and multiple coding sessions?
* What should I be doing myself to become a better developer instead of becoming overly dependent on AI?

I'm still figuring this out, and I'm sure we're making plenty of mistakes. I'd love to hear how others approach this process or projects.             (Like how do you handle asset production with what pipeline for what kind of art design?)

comments.author: Bavariasnaps
comments.body: Did you ever made a protoype thats actually fun to play? Did you show it to real humans, testers, and watched their reaction? This is what a game developer would do. This is where AI will not help you.

replies.author: Thrustherx
replies.body: I haven't progressed that far but I am playing it every step and making changes accordingly. Hardest part so far is creating assets-visuals as the stronger models like opus and fable spend my limit very quickly. I want to learn if there is an alternative or am I supposed to do it this way. I am trying to be consistent with them and not just telling it to one shot. So I have tons of grayboxes and testing environments

comments.author: Radiant_Mind33
comments.body:
In theory you have more control by aiming at smaller tasks. But it can turn into a quagmire where you are practically guaranteed to lose consistency over time.  It's not like there's a choice though. No agent can just build it all and keep all of that in context. 

Most of us probably don't manage context anymore. Meaning we just start one new focused chat for one task. Then move to another chat immediately after. Unless you don't care about making the most out of the 5-hour usage windows, this is the way. And sure some tasks aren't done that quickly, but still. The point is not to explode the context window.

If your agents need the whole context every time there's something fundamentally wrong with the workflow. I.E, YOU who must not actually understand your own creation. lmao.

replies.author: Thrustherx
replies.body: I am just a bit overwhelmed, I havent surpassed any context but I am guessing I could use the memory and tokens more efficiently, just sometimes i get lost hence I am here to seek suggestions
